Warden's note, women's hostel, second floor.
This term I've watched Kalyani look after her friend Urmila, who has been struggling since her grandmother died. Kalyani doesn't lecture. She never says "at least" or "I went through worse." She sits on the end of Urmila's bed in the evenings, sometimes talking, sometimes just doing her own homework beside her.
She brings Urmila's lab notes back from class and makes sure there's a plate of rice waiting after mess hours. She knocks every morning to check in.
Last week Urmila snapped, "Stop hovering, you're not my mother." Kalyani looked hurt and left. But she came back the next evening anyway, with tea.
Yesterday Kalyani came to me. "I'm not a counsellor. I think she needs someone trained." We agreed she would suggest it gently to Urmila. This morning Urmila asked me for the campus counsellor's number.

qa.q: What does Kalyani make sure is waiting after mess hours?
qa.a: A plate of rice.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when Urmila told her to stop hovering?
qa.a: She felt hurt and stung, and left, but her care won out and she came back the next evening with tea.

qa.q: Which parts of Kalyani's support worked well?
qa.a: Listening, checking in, keeping Urmila company, practical help with notes and food, no lectures or comparing pain, and recognising she isn't a therapist so she nudged Urmila toward professional care.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel about Kalyani's evening visits?
qa.a: She may sometimes feel crowded or resentful, but also less alone and cared for, which helped her ask for the counsellor.

grounding: A warden observes Kalyani listening, checking in, offering company and practical help without lecturing, and nudging her grieving friend toward professional care.

Zubin had shared a flat in Bandra with Payal for a year, and lately he'd started worrying about her.
Every night around one, her phone buzzed. It was always Rhea, her college friend, crying about her breakup and exam stress. Payal would sit on the balcony talking until three. She'd started missing her morning lectures. At breakfast she looked grey.
One morning Zubin found her asleep on the sofa, phone on her chest. When she woke, she said, "I'm so tired. But if I don't pick up, I feel like a terrible friend."
Zubin made her tea. "You can care about Rhea and still sleep. Who else does she have?"
"Her sister. The college counsellor, maybe."
"What if you told Rhea you'll talk before eleven, and help her reach them too?"
Payal was quiet. Then she typed the message, and switched her phone to silent at midnight.

qa.q: What time did Payal's phone usually buzz?
qa.a: Around one every night.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling as he watched Payal over those weeks?
qa.a: He felt worried and protective, seeing her exhausted and missing lectures.

qa.q: What did Zubin suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Setting a kind limit on call times and involving Rhea's sister and the college counsellor, so Payal can keep helping without burning out.

qa.q: How does Payal feel about the late-night calls?
qa.a: She feels drained and guilty, afraid that not answering would make her a terrible friend.

grounding: Zubin notices his flatmate becoming a friend's only support and feeling drained and guilty, and helps her set kind limits and involve others.

Maria had moved to Pune for work, and her best friend Anjali was back in Kochi, having a terrible year. In exam week, when Maria's own deadlines were piling up, she finally called.
"Just leave me alone, Maria," Anjali said, and hung up.
Maria stared at the phone. It felt like a slap. Part of her was angry. I've been trying for months. Fine.
But she remembered what Anjali's mother had told her: Anjali was safe at home and seeing a doctor, just very low.
So Maria didn't push, and she didn't disappear. Every few days she sent something small. "No need to reply. Saw a boat like the one we took in Alleppey. Thinking of you." Then, "Still here whenever."
Nine days later, a message came. "Sorry I was rude. Can we talk Sunday?" Maria smiled and wrote, "Always."

qa.q: How many days later did Anjali's message come?
qa.a: Nine days later.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when Anjali hung up?
qa.a: She felt rejected and angry, as if she'd been slapped after months of trying.

qa.q: What did Maria do that kept the door open?
qa.a: She respected Anjali's pace, knowing Anjali was safe, and stayed gently reachable with small no-pressure messages.

qa.q: How might Anjali see Maria's small messages?
qa.a: She probably felt cared for without being pushed, and came to admire her friend's patience, which made it easier to reply.

grounding: Maria feels rejected when her friend says leave me alone, but stays gently reachable with low-pressure messages and respects her pace, knowing she is safe.

You asked what the hardest part of this year was, Sudha. Honestly? It was seeing Appa like that. I'm Ojas, the elder one, and I was always the one Appa worried about, not the other way round.
After he retired, he stopped reading the paper, stopped going for walks, sat in his chair all day. Amma was frantic, calling me every night.
Suddenly I was the parent. I was scared something was really wrong, and guilty that I lived two hours away. For weeks I just absorbed it, said nothing, lay awake.
Then one Sunday I sat next to him. "Appa, I love you. You don't seem like yourself. Can we see Dr Menon together?" He grumbled. But he went.
And then I called you. Remember? I said, "I can't do this alone." You took the Tuesday calls with Amma. That changed everything, Sudha.

qa.q: Which doctor did Ojas suggest Appa see?
qa.a: Dr Menon.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when Appa withdrew after retiring?
qa.a: Ojas felt frightened that something was really wrong and guilty about living two hours away, like the roles had reversed.

qa.q: What helped more than silently absorbing it?
qa.a: Speaking to Appa with love, suggesting a doctor visit together and sharing the load with Sudha.

qa.q: What would change if Ojas had kept absorbing everything alone?
qa.a: Ojas might have burned out, Appa might not have seen a doctor, and Sudha would never have been asked to share the Tuesday calls with Amma.

grounding: Ojas sees Appa withdrawn and Amma worried, feels role reversal, fear and guilt, and speaks with love, suggests a doctor and shares the load with a sibling.

Mehak, your mother says she's fine, doesn't she? Your Seema Aunty heard those same words from my own father when I was twenty-five.
After my mother died, Papa stopped eating properly, stopped sleeping, and snapped at everyone. When I said "counsellor," he went red. "Am I mad? What will the neighbours say?"
So I tried a different way. I said, "Papa, you're not sleeping, you've lost your appetite. That's your health. Let's show Dr Rao." Dr Rao had treated him for thirty years; Papa trusted him.
I let Papa go in alone first, so he kept his pride. Dr Rao talked to him about sleep and grief, and then, gently, about a counsellor his clinic worked with.
Papa went. He never told the neighbours, and I never asked him to. So, Mehak, call it health, bring in someone she trusts, and let her keep her dignity.

qa.q: How long had Dr Rao treated Seema Aunty's father?
qa.a: Thirty years.

qa.q: How did young Seema's father feel when she mentioned a counsellor?
qa.a: He felt insulted and anxious, going red and worrying he'd be seen as mad and what the neighbours would say.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made him accept help?
qa.a: Seema framed it as health, involved Dr Rao, whom he trusted, and let him go in alone to keep his dignity.

qa.q: How might Dr Rao have seen his old patient that day?
qa.a: Dr Rao likely saw a grieving man who needed gentle care, and used that long trust to suggest a counsellor.

grounding: Seema Aunty tells how her father resisted help out of fear of gossip, and framing it as health, a trusted family doctor and respect for dignity helped him accept.

The visitors' room at the Ernakulam day-care centre for older people was quiet at four. Binita watched her father, Thomas, sign out Ammachi, his hands trembling. For two years he had cared for his mother alone since her memory began to fail.
"Pappa, when did you last sleep a full night?" Binita asked.
He laughed tiredly. "What is full?"
"Have you eaten today?"
"Tea."
Binita took the bag from him. She'd been noticing for weeks. That evening she made a list. She would take Ammachi on Tuesdays and Saturdays. Her brother would pay for a night helper twice a week. She asked the centre's social worker about a caregivers' support group and booked Pappa a check-up with his own doctor.
But she kept her Thursday evenings for her dance class. "If I burn out, Pappa, we both fall," she told him. He nodded, and for the first time didn't argue.

qa.q: Which evenings did Binita keep for herself?
qa.a: Her Thursday evenings, for her dance class.

qa.q: How was Thomas feeling after two years of caring alone?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and worn down, not sleeping properly and barely eating, with trembling hands.

qa.q: What did Binita get right as a family member helping the caregiver?
qa.a: She checked his sleep and meals, shared tasks with her brother, sought professional support and a check-up, and protected her own life to avoid burnout.

qa.q: How might Ammachi's days change with Binita's plan?
qa.a: She would still be cared for, but by a less exhausted son and a wider circle, which may make her days calmer and safer.

grounding: Binita checks her caregiver father's sleep, meals and health, shares tasks, seeks professional support and protects her own life to avoid burnout.

Today at recess Rohan pointed at Elizabeth talking to herself on the swing and said, "Paagal!" Everyone laughed. Then someone said her mummy goes to a mad doctor. Elizabeth ran to the washroom.
I didn't laugh. But my stomach hurt. Because last month I cried a lot at night and didn't tell anyone. Now I think if I tell, they'll call me paagal too.
At dinner Chachu said Anand Uncle is "weak in the head" because he went to a hospital for his worry. I didn't eat my roti.
Later, Amma came to my bed. She said feelings can get sick like a stomach can, and that she saw a counsellor after Nani died, and it helped. "No one in this house is paagal for being sad," she said.
So I told her about the crying. She hugged me and said we'd talk to someone together.
Lakshmi

qa.a: "Paagal!"

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi's stomach hurt after recess?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt hurt and scared, and ashamed of the secret crying, fearing being called paagal too.

qa.q: How did Amma protect Lakshmi from hiding pain?
qa.a: By speaking openly about feelings as health, sharing her own counselling after Nani died, and saying no one is paagal for being sad.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel in the washroom?

grounding: Lakshmi hears classmates and family mock mental health struggles and learns to hide pain, until Amma speaks openly about feelings and health.

The house in Ludhiana was full of aunties for Jasleen's sister's engagement, and everyone was talking about the boy's family. So when the school counsellor's reminder buzzed on her phone for Thursday, Jasleen quickly hid it.
Mummy had said it clearly: "No one outside this house knows about the counselling. Log kya kahenge? Your sister's rishta could break."
So Jasleen smiled at every aunty and said she was "fine, just exams." Inside she felt more alone than ever. At night she lay awake, anxious someone would find out.
Her cousin Deepak found her on the terrace while the others were dancing. "You look like you're somewhere else."
She hesitated. Deepak had always kept her secrets. "I see a counsellor. For my anxiety. Nobody can know."
Deepak just sat down beside her. "That's good. I'm glad you have someone." Jasleen felt her shoulders loosen. For the first time in weeks, she wasn't carrying it alone.

qa.q: Where did Deepak find Jasleen?
qa.a: On the terrace, while the others were dancing.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel while hiding the counselling from the aunties?
qa.a: She felt lonely and anxious, lying awake at night worried someone would find out.

qa.q: What choice brought Jasleen relief, and why?
qa.a: Choosing to tell a trusted person, Deepak, who had always kept her secrets; sharing eased the loneliness that the secrecy caused.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the counselling differently if gossip weren't a worry?
qa.a: She might feel free to support Jasleen openly and proud she's getting help, instead of fearing for the rishta.

grounding: Jasleen hides her counselling from relatives to avoid gossip and marriage worries, feels lonely, and finds relief by telling a trusted cousin.

"Pradeep, you've been off since Monday. Everything okay?" Rekha asked, pulling a chair up to his desk.
"Just... tired. Stressed. It's nothing."
"Okay. You don't have to tell me anything." She paused. "But I'll share something, since I'm comfortable with it. Last year I saw a psychiatrist for panic attacks. Same way I saw a physio for my knee."
Pradeep looked up. "You? You're the calmest person here."
"Now, yes. Treatment helped. That's all."
"I didn't know people here talked about that."
"Most don't. But I don't think it should be a secret, any more than a fever is."
"I think I might need to talk to someone," he said quietly.
"The company helpline is on the notice board. Want me to send you the number?"
"Yes. Thanks, Rekha."
"Anytime." She squeezed his shoulder, not with pity, just like a colleague, and went back to her desk.

qa.q: What did Rekha compare seeing a psychiatrist to?
qa.a: Seeing a physio for her knee.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when Rekha shared her story?
qa.a: He felt surprised and then relieved, seeing that even the calmest person had struggled, which made asking for help feel possible.

qa.q: What did Rekha get right in this conversation?
qa.a: She shared only because she was comfortable, treated mental health like physical health, offered a practical next step and supported him without pity.

qa.q: How might Rekha's openness affect others in the office?
qa.a: It may make it easier for the next person to ask for help, because one respectful conversation makes the topic less of a secret.

grounding: Rekha shares her own experience when comfortable, treats mental health like physical health and supports a colleague without pity, making it easier for him to seek help.
